newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-JONES GIVES U.S. NEW STAR.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JONES GIVES U.S. NEW STAR.

text.p: With 100-meter sprints and a long jump unequalled in the world this year, new U.S. star Marion Jones boldly grabbed two berths on America's world championship team.
Deciding the status of several other American stars for the IAAF title meet may be more complicated.

While the 21-year-old Jones emerged from the U.S. championships that ended here on Sunday as a strong contender for women's 100-meter and long jump gold at August's world championships, injured Americans Michael Johnson, Dan O'Brien, Gwen Torrence and Gail Devers must await off-the-track action to determine their eligibilty for Athens.

The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF), mindful of the potential absence of injured Atlanta Olympics hero Johnson to its showcase meeting, is considering "wild card" entries to all world record-holders and defending world champions. That would put Johnson and the other injured Americans in the meet along with marquee names not selected by their national federations.
"The championships would have a hollow ring without Johnson, because right now he is track and field to many people," said Garry Hill, editor of Track & Field News magazine.
Such an unprecedented move would swell an American team of fresh faces and seasoned veterans already selected by head-to-head competetion.

Maurice Greene and Tim Montgomery, never before factors in major championships, headline a revamped U.S. 100-meter corps. There's also newcomer Melissa Morrison, the year's fastest women's 100-meter hurdler, and young 400-meter runners Tyree Washington and Jerome Young.
No one produced a bigger surprise, though, than Jones, who had been absent from the sport for almost two years while playing college basketball and recovering from a twice-broken left foot.

"Marion Jones now looks like what we thought she would five years ago," said Hill of the former California high school star. "We said then she was going to be the world's best sprinter and long jumper. Now, if she's not, she's looking very much like it.
"She definitely stands out as the revelation of the meet, men or women."
Hill, however, would not call the appearance of a relatively large number of newcomers on the team "a changing of the guard."
"I suspect it's more of a post-Olympic letdown. There are a lot of tired people who had to get up big in '95 for the world championships and get up big in '96 for the Olympics," he said.
"Still I would not suspect the U.S. share of gold medals to change much (from the 1995 world championships)," he added.
Olympic champions Allen Johnson, Derrick Adkins, Charles Austin, Kenny Harrison and Randy Barnes and women's 400-meter hurdles world record-holder Kim Batten will likely ensure that.
